Dunghill
DUNG-hil
noun
A plain English compound of dung and hill — the heap of refuse and manure outside a house or city. It renders the Hebrew ashpoth, a rubbish heap, and the Aramaic nevalu, a ruin or dunghill; the lowest and filthiest place a man could be found.

Biblical Definition

The dunghill is the refuse heap outside the gate, where the sweepings of a city and the dung of its beasts were cast, and where the destitute lay because there was nowhere lower to go. Scripture uses it almost always to measure a distance. Hannah sings it first: “He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory” (1Sa 2:8). The Psalmist takes up her line and repeats it as settled doctrine about the character of God: “He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth the needy out of the dunghill” (Psa 113:7), and the next verse says why — that he may set him with princes. Jeremiah measures a fall by the same heap: they that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets, and they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills (Lam 4:5). Daniel records the Chaldean threat to make a man’s house a dunghill, and Christ Himself ends His parable of savourless salt there — it is neither fit for the land, nor yet for the dunghill; but men cast it out (Luk 14:35). Below the dunghill there is nothing. That is exactly why the LORD is said to reach into it: the beggar is not lifted from a promising position but from the refuse, and the throne of glory is at the other end of that lift.

Webster 1828 Definition

A heap of dung and refuse cast outside a dwelling or city; hence any mean, vile, or lowest situation.

expand to see more

DUNGHILL, a heap of dung; a place where dung and the refuse of a house or city are laid.

Any mean or vile abode or condition; a place of filth and contempt.

As an adjective, sprung from the dunghill; mean; low; base.

A plain compound of dung and hill, rendering the Hebrew ashpoth, a rubbish heap.

Hannah and the Psalmist both make it the place from which God lifts the beggar to sit among princes (1Sa 2:8; Psa 113:7).

Key Scripture

1Sa 2:8 — "He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD'S, and he hath set the world upon them."

Psa 113:7 — "He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth the needy out of the dunghill;"

Lam 4:5 — "They that did feed delicately are desolate in the streets: they that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills."

Luk 14:35 — "It is neither fit for the land, nor yet for the dunghill; but men cast it out. He that hath ears to hear, let him hear."

Modern Corruption

Hannah’s song is regularly read as a manifesto of social reversal; it is a confession of sovereign grace — the LORD Himself lifts a particular beggar from a particular dunghill because it pleases Him to do it.

expand to see more

Liberation theology and its evangelical imitators have made 1 Samuel 2 and the Magnificat that echoes it into a political programme: the poor as a class are the subject, reversal is the plot, and the church’s business is to bring the reversal about. The text will not sit still for it. Hannah is not describing a movement; she is describing a Person, and every verb belongs to Him — the LORD killeth and maketh alive, He bringeth low and lifteth up, He raiseth the poor, He lifteth the beggar, He setteth them among princes. The reason given in the same verse is not economic but metaphysical: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD’S, and He hath set the world upon them. He may lift whom He will because He owns the ground. Strip that out and Hannah’s song becomes a slogan; leave it in and it is the doctrine of sovereign, particular, undeserved grace sung by a woman who had been barren and was now a mother.

Recover the personal edge of the verse, for that is where its comfort lies. The dunghill is where a man is found by grace, not where he is left. Scripture is candid about what we bring to the transaction — our righteousnesses are as filthy rags, and Paul counted his best religious credentials as dung that he might win Christ. That is the same heap. The gospel does not say that God saw promise in the beggar; it says the LORD lifted him from the refuse and set him among princes and gave him to inherit the throne of glory, and Job is the picture of it, sitting down among the ashes and raised up at the last. The doctrine humbles a man before it exalts him, and it keeps him humble after, because a prince who remembers the dunghill has nothing to boast of but the hand that reached in.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The refuse heap outside the gate — the lowest place a man can lie, and the place from which God lifts beggars to sit with princes.

expand to see more

Dunghill — a plain compound of dung and hill, the refuse heap of a house or city.

Hebrew ashpoth, a rubbish heap; Aramaic nevalu, a ruin.

Hannah sings that the LORD lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill (1Sa 2:8).

The Psalmist repeats it as settled doctrine of God’s character (Psa 113:7).

Savourless salt is fit neither for the land nor for the dunghill (Luk 14:35).

Usage

"He lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill — the verb belongs wholly to the LORD."

"They that were brought up in scarlet embrace dunghills: the measure of a fall."

"A prince who remembers the dunghill has nothing left to boast of."
